title: Reading plans: seq/index/index-only/bitmap scans, nested loop/hash/merge joins
summary: The planner picks one of four ways to read each table and one of three ways to join each pair, per query, from estimated row counts. Each choice tells you what it believed; EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells you whether it was right.

examples.title: One table, six plans: seq, index, index-only, bitmap, BitmapOr, ordered

annotations.note: value is a scrambled permutation (the 7919 trick from the previous lesson) and sensor_id repeats every 200 rows: neither follows the physical order of the table.

90% of the rows match, so the planner reads every page once and tests the Filter on each row. A Seq Scan is always on the menu; every other plan needs an index that matches the condition or the ORDER BY.
Index Scan: descend the tree, then fetch each match from the table. Unbeatable for a handful of rows, expensive per row for many.

Index Only Scan: the query needs only id, and the index holds it, so the table can be skipped for pages the visibility map marks all-visible. B-trees always support this; GiST and SP-GiST only for some operator classes; GIN never, because its entries hold only parts of the values.

Bitmap scan: 200 matches scattered over the table. The bitmap orders their locations by page, so each page is read once, in physical order. That also means the index order is lost: an ORDER BY on top of a bitmap scan needs its own Sort.

A single index scan can only use conditions joined by AND on its own columns. Here each index builds a bitmap and BitmapOr merges them. AND conditions on two indexes combine the same way (BitmapAnd), though one composite index usually beats that (next lesson).
No Sort node: the index hands rows over in value order, and Limit stops pulling after five. The cost is the same on 20,000 rows or 20 million, which is what keyset pagination (lesson 5) builds on.

Heap Fetches: 100. The visibility map of a brand-new table has no bits set (VACUUM sets them, and these uncommitted rows aren't visible to anyone else anyway), so every row is checked in the table. Only 3 buffers, because the 100 rows share one heap page next to 2 index pages. On a vacuumed table that changes slowly, Heap Fetches drops toward 0, and only then does index-only pay off.

examples.title: The three join methods, each where it fits

annotations.note: Ten orders per customer, scattered over the table. The index on orders.customer_id is explicit: a foreign key doesn't create one.

Nested Loop: the first child (outer) yields 3 customers; the second child (inner) runs once per outer row with that row's id plugged in, which is why its Index Cond mentions c.id. The IN list became = ANY(array), a single index scan for all three keys.

Hash Join: the Hash node reads customers once into an in-memory hash table keyed on id, then all 20,000 orders stream past it. No index needed, each table read once. HashAggregate then groups by city with a second hash table.

Merge Join: both inputs arrive sorted on the join key (customers from its primary key, orders from orders_customer), so one merge pass joins them, and the result is already in c.id order: no Sort node for the ORDER BY.

examples.title: One join, three methods: what the rejected plans would have cost

annotations.note: The same tables as before, but now 500 customers qualify: too many for one index lookup each, so the planner hashes them instead.

120 buffers: customers' 11 pages and orders' 109, each read once. Batches: 1 means the hash table fit in memory; the limit is work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier (4MB × 2.0 by default), and a hash table past it spills to temporary files in more batches. Planning: Buffers counts pages the planner itself read while choosing.

Nested Loop, forced: the inner Index Scan ran 500 times (loops=500, Index Searches: 500). actual rows=10.00 is per loop, so 5,000 rows in total. Each loop reads 2 index pages and 10 table pages: 6,011 page accesses, 50 times the hash join. With 3 outer rows (previous example) the same shape was the cheapest plan; the method depends on the row counts, not on the query text.

Merge Join, forced: customers gets an explicit Sort (500 rows in memory), orders comes sorted from its index at one page jump per row: 20,005 accesses. It reads 19,981 orders and stops: past the last İzmir customer (id 1998) there's nothing left to merge.
All three methods off, and a join is still required. enable_* only discourages, so the planner takes the cheapest disabled plan and PG 18 marks it Disabled: true; older versions printed no marker.

use_cases: Diagnosing a slow endpoint: find the node where actual rows, loops or buffers explode, and compare its actual rows with the estimate
Deciding between a composite index and two single-column indexes combined with BitmapAnd
Checking that ORDER BY ... LIMIT stops early on an index instead of sorting the whole table
Explaining why one customer's page is fast and a whole city's report is slow: the join method changes with the row counts
strengths: The algorithm is chosen per query from statistics: the same join is a nested loop for 3 customers and a hash join for 500, which a hand-written loop in Go or an ORM can't do
Bitmap scans combine any number of single-column indexes for AND/OR conditions and still read each table page only once
Index order replaces sorting: index scans and merge joins deliver ordered rows, so ORDER BY ... LIMIT can stop after a few rows
Rejected alternatives are measurable: switch a method off with SET LOCAL and compare buffers in the same transaction
weaknesses: Every choice is only as good as the row estimates: a nested loop planned for 3 outer rows that meets 50,000 is the classic slow query
Core PostgreSQL has no per-query hints; the enable_* switches are coarse and apply to everything in the session or transaction
Index-only scans depend on the visibility map, so on a busy table they degrade into index scans until VACUUM catches up
Hashes and sorts are bounded per node by work_mem (hashes: times hash_mem_multiplier) and spill to temporary files beyond it

pitfalls.title: Reading actual rows without loops
pitfalls.detail: On the inner side of a nested loop, actual rows is the average per execution. rows=10.00 loops=500 is 5,000 rows. Multiply before comparing with the estimate or blaming the node.

pitfalls.title: Reading Buffers as per-node work
pitfalls.detail: A node's Buffers include all of its children. The Aggregate's 120 in the hash join plan is the two Seq Scans' 11 + 109, not 120 more.

pitfalls.title: Expecting an index-only scan right after a bulk load
pitfalls.detail: Until VACUUM has set the visibility map, every row is checked in the table (Heap Fetches). After a large load, vacuum and analyze explicitly instead of waiting for autovacuum.

pitfalls.title: Raising work_mem server-wide for one report
pitfalls.detail: work_mem applies per sort or hash node, per session, so a global increase multiplies across every concurrent query. Raise it for the one transaction that needs it.
pitfalls.good: BEGIN; SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'; SELECT ...; COMMIT;

quiz.q: An inner Index Scan shows `actual rows=10.00 loops=500`. How many rows did it produce in total?
quiz.why: Actual rows is the per-loop average; multiply by loops.

quiz.q: Why does a Bitmap Heap Scan need a separate Sort for ORDER BY, even on an indexed column?
options: It visits rows in physical page order, so the index order is lost
quiz.why: The bitmap is laid out by page so each page is read once; the docs note that any ordering of the original indexes is lost.

quiz.q: An Index Only Scan reports `Heap Fetches` equal to the number of rows. What usually fixes it in a real database?
options: VACUUM, so the visibility map marks pages all-visible
quiz.why: The table can be skipped only for all-visible pages, and VACUUM is what records them.

quiz.q: You join every row of two large tables on a key with no index, and the output order doesn't matter. Which method do you expect?
quiz.why: One pass over each table, no index or sort needed. A nested loop would rescan the inner side per row; a merge join would have to sort both sides first.

body:
## Concept

For each table in a query the planner considers a **Seq Scan** (always possible) and an
index-based scan for every index whose columns match a condition or the `ORDER BY`. For
each pair of inputs it considers three join methods. It estimates the cost of the
combinations and runs the cheapest. The menu:

- **Seq Scan**: every page, once, in order. Right for a large fraction of the table.
- **Index Scan**: descend, then one table fetch per match. Right for a few rows, or when
  the index order saves a sort.
- **Index Only Scan**: answer from the index alone, for pages the visibility map marks
  all-visible.
- **Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan**: collect matching locations first, read each
  page once in physical order. The middle ground, and the way to combine indexes.
- **Nested Loop**: for each outer row, run the inner side. Right when the outer side is
  small and the inner side has an index.
- **Hash Join**: build a hash table on one side, stream the other. Right for large,
  unsorted inputs.
- **Merge Join**: walk two inputs sorted on the key. Right when both arrive sorted, or the
  output must be sorted anyway.

None of them is good or bad by itself. A plan is a statement about row counts: a nested
loop says "the outer side is small". Your job when reading it is to check that belief.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

You've written all three joins by hand:

- **Nested loop:** `for c in customers: for o in index[c.id]` in Python, or a lookup in a
  `TreeMap` per outer element in Java. Without the index it is JS's
  `customers.map(c => orders.filter(o => o.customerId === c.id))`, O(n·m).
- **Hash join:** build a `HashMap<Integer, Customer>` (Go: `map[int]Customer`) from the
  smaller list, then loop over the larger one and probe it.
- **Merge join:** the merge step of merge sort, over two lists sorted by the same key.

The difference is that you choose once, when you write the code, while the planner
chooses per execution from estimated sizes. An ORM that loads customers and then queries
each one's orders is running a nested loop from the application, with a network round
trip per inner lookup: the N+1 problem of lesson 5.

## How it works

Reading `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` output, node by node:

- **`actual rows=10.00 loops=500`**: rows are averages per loop. Since PG 18 they are
  printed with two decimals, because an average needn't be whole.
- **`Index Searches: 500`** (new in PG 18): descents of the tree across all loops. On the
  inner side of a nested loop that's one per outer row. A range is one search; an
  `= ANY(...)` list can take up to one per element, fewer when neighbouring keys share a
  leaf page.
- **`Buffers`**: cumulative, a node's count includes its children's.
- **Hash**: `Buckets`, `Batches`, `Memory Usage`. One batch means it fit in memory.
- **Sort**: `Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 25kB` fit in `work_mem`; `external merge
  Disk: ...` did not.
- **`Heap Fetches`**: table visits an index-only scan couldn't skip.
- **`Rows Removed by Filter`**: rows read and thrown away; a large number on a selective
  query is the classic sign of a missing or unusable index.

Two more nodes you'll meet: **Memoize** (PG 14+) sits between a nested loop and its inner
scan and caches inner results per key when the same keys repeat; **Gather** with
`Parallel Seq Scan` below it means the work was split across worker processes, which
starts once a table passes `min_parallel_table_scan_size` (8 MB by default).

## Design notes

Read a slow plan in this order:

1. Find the node with the largest actual rows × loops, or the largest Buffers.
2. Compare its actual rows with the estimate (`EXPLAIN` without `COSTS OFF`). A tenfold
   gap is the usual root cause: the planner picked a nested loop for "3 rows" and got
   thousands. Fix the estimate (`ANALYZE`, extended statistics, lesson 5) before
   anything else.
3. If the estimate is right and the plan is still slow, the fix is an index that matches
   the query (lesson 3) or a different query shape.

`enable_*` switches belong between steps 2 and 3: confirming what the alternative would
cost, as in the third example. The docs call them a crude method and a temporary
solution, and core PostgreSQL has no per-query hints. A plan you had to force today
breaks silently when the data changes tomorrow; a correct estimate keeps adapting.
